headline: 53 Orangutans Rescued From Borneo Fires, Given New Lives in Protected Forests
meta_description: An Indonesian nonprofit has rescued 53 critically endangered orangutans from devastating wildfires in Borneo, with many rewilded to forest preserves across the…
summary_short: Since August, a primate rescue nonprofit has saved 53 orangutans from Borneo's wildfires, including stressed mothers and infants, and is rewilding survivors to protected…
body:
Since August, devastating wildfires across Borneo have destroyed vast tracts of forest and peatland, leaving critically endangered orangutans without food or shelter. In response, YIARI—an 18-year-old nonprofit dedicated to primate rescue and conservation in Indonesia—has rescued 53 orangutans from the fires, with many now being rewilded to forest preserves across the island. The team has worked around the clock, responding to urgent cases of stranded animals, orphaned mothers and infants found in critical condition, and relocating survivors to protected areas like Gunung Palung National Park, located five hours away. Among the rescued is a young orangutan named Irene, who arrived malnourished and visibly stressed after days without food in the devastated landscape. Dr. Karmele Llano Sanchez, YIARI's CEO and a wildlife veterinarian, has personally overseen the care of these animals during recovery.

Many of the rescued orangutans remain under veterinary care at YIARI's Rehabilitation Centre as the team continues to patrol fire-affected areas and respond to distress calls. Yet success brings a new challenge: the centre has reached full capacity. The organization is now seeking public donations to sustain its critical work and expand its ability to help more animals. International Animal Rescue, which partners with YIARI, believes the recovery efforts reveal something profound about our connection to these animals—their movements and facial expressions remind us just how similar we are to them.

As seasonal rains finally arrive, delayed from October into November, there is cautious hope that the delayed precipitation will help extinguish the remaining blazes and allow Borneo's forests to begin healing.
